added: #Insulate your basement with fire-blocking materials. Insulators like gypsum, mineral wool and particle board are known for their fire-retardant qualities. If you’re in the process of building a new house, you probably won’t have to specify that you want fireproof materials, as these features are now standard. That being said, it never hurts to ask what types of materials are being used in the construction of your home.[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#*It’s also critical that your basement present some clear and unobstructed means of escape in case a fire does break out. Your windows will need to be at least 20" wide by 24" high and easy to open without any screens, grills or other covers.

#*It’s also critical that your basement present some clear and unobstructed means of escape in case a fire does break out. Your windows will need to be at least 20" wide by 24" high and easy to open without any screens, grills or other covers.<ref>http://news.nationalpost.com/homes/mike-holmes-how-to-turn-your-basement-into-a-proper-rental-apartment</ref>

added: #Measure the distance between your basement wall studs. Stretch a tape measure across the expanse from one stud to another. You should be measuring between the inner edges of the studs. Write this number down, rounding to the nearest quarter inch (roughly 1.25cm) The firestopping blocks will be cut to fit this space.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pWvBEwRitbE</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Cut 2x4s to fit the space between each stud. Acquire a set of 2” (48mm) nominal lumber boards. Using the measurements of the stud spacing that you just took, saw the boards straight across width-wise. Take care to make the edges clean and even. The best way to do this is to use a circular saw that allows you to make precise cuts.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/tools/circular-saws/circular-saw-tips-and-techniques/view-all</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Secure the firestopping blocks. Position the newly made blocks in the space at the top of the studs where they meet the floor joists or recessed wall frame. Nail the blocks into place, then test them to confirm that they’re firmly fastened.[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Treat the blocks with a fire retardant coating. This coating can prevent a fire from burning through your blocks and spreading. Firestopping blocks can only withstand a standard fire for a certain period of time, often just 15 minutes. A fire retardant coating can extend that time.[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Fill in the gaps with fireproof caulking. If there are any spaces remaining between the studs and the firestopping blocks, this will seal them and prevent drafts from forming and accelerating the spread of fire. Simply spray a thin line into whatever cracks and crevices you come across. As it dries, the caulk will expand inside the gaps, blocking them off and neutralizing airflow. <ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F9_fHgUx3b0</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Wall over the studs. Once the firestopping blocks have been successfully installed, you can proceed to cover the studs with plywood or drywall. This will create multiple separate compartments inside the wall rather than one large cavity. In the event of an emergency, each individual compartment will help stop or slow the spread of fire.<ref>http://www.askthebuilder.com/fire-stop-construction/</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 6 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Insulate your basement with fire-blocking materials. Insulators like gypsum, mineral wool and particle board are known for their fire-retardant qualities. If you’re in the process of building a new house, you probably won’t have to specify that you want fireproof materials, as these features are now standard. That being said, it never hurts to ask what types of materials are being used in the construction of your home.<ref>http://www.pdskc.org/portals/pdskc/documents/applications_forms/checklists/BasementHandout.pdf</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Use fireproof caulking and adhesives. As mentioned, there are many different types of sealants available that have been approved for firestopping. Use fireproof caulking to seal any visible cracks or spaces between firestopping blocks, wall studs and joists. It only takes a small amount to make problem areas fire-tight.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pWvBEwRitbE</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 8 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Invest in fire-safe windows. For basements with windows, you’ll want to shop around for styles that meet prescribed safety regulations. You can also pick out windows that are made with fire-rated glass. These types of window glasses are treated with special compounds that reflect and disperse heat, making them less likely to shatter. With the right windows, you’ll be protected from fire whether it originates inside or outside.<ref>https://www.thisoldhouse.com/ideas/fire-resistant-doors-and-windows</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 9 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Install a home sprinkler system. While not a form of fireproofing in the traditional sense, a sprinkler system can stop flames in their tracks before they grow big enough to wreak havoc. Sprinklers trigger automatically when exposed to heat, meaning you don’t even have to be aware of a fire for them to do their job. This makes them an exceptional first line of defense against fires that start in the sub-levels of your home.<ref>https://www.thisoldhouse.com/ideas/fire-resistant-insulation-and-systems</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 10 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Have your wiring inspected regularly. Faulty electrical wiring is one of the leading causes of household fires. Schedule an inspection at least once a year to to ensure that your home’s wiring is safe. In the meantime, be on the lookout for fraying, splitting, shorting and other electrical risks that could potentially lead to a fire.<ref>https://sewelldirect.com/learning-center/cable-fire-safety</ref>[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 11.jpg|center]]

#Place fire extinguishers in easily accessed areas. In the event of a small fire, a fire extinguisher can be a great asset. Show everyone in the family where your fire extinguishers are located. Make sure each person also knows how to use them.[[Image:Fireproof a Basement Step 12.jpg|center]]

#*You can also use 2x8s (48mm x 198mm) if a wider space exists between the studs and the foundation wall.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pWvBEwRitbE</ref>
#*Nominal lumber is one of a few firestopping materials approved by the International Residential Code (IRC).

#Secure the firestopping blocks. Position the newly made blocks in the space at the top of the studs where they meet the floor joists or recessed wall frame. Nail the blocks into place, then test them to confirm that they’re firmly fastened.
#*To be on the safe side, seal every space surrounding the blocks, including where the studs intersect the joists of the upper floor.

#Use fireproof caulking and adhesives. As mentioned, there are many different types of sealants available that have been approved for firestopping. Use fireproof caulking to seal any visible cracks or spaces between firestopping blocks, wall studs and joists. It only takes a small amount to make problem areas fire-tight.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pWvBEwRitbE</ref>
#*Finishing your basement with a fireproof sealant is always a good idea, especially if your home has balloon framing or a similarly hollow construction that can create openings for drafts.

#Invest in fire-safe windows. For basements with windows, you’ll want to shop around for styles that meet prescribed safety regulations. You can also pick out windows that are made with fire-rated glass. These types of window glasses are treated with special compounds that reflect and disperse heat, making them less likely to shatter. With the right windows, you’ll be protected from fire whether it originates inside or outside.<ref>https://www.thisoldhouse.com/ideas/fire-resistant-doors-and-windows</ref>

#*It’s also critical that your basement present some clear and unobstructed means of escape in case a fire does break out. Your windows will need to be at least 20" wide by 24" high and easy to open without any screens, grills or other covers.<ref>http://news.nationalpost.com/homes/mike-holmes-how-to-turn-your-basement-into-a-proper-rental-apartment</ref>

added: Fire safety should be a major concern for any domicile, old or new. If you’re intent on fireproofing your home’s basement but dread the time, expense and inconvenience it entails, you’ll be relieved to learn that the process doesn’t have to be as difficult as you think. New homes under construction often employ firestopping blocks that prevent flames from spreading to other parts of the house, while older homes can be outfitted with other easy-to-install fireproofing measures. Finding an option that works for your living space could save both your property and your life.
== Steps ==
=== Installing Firestopping Blocks ===

#Measure the distance between your basement wall studs. Stretch a tape measure across the expanse from one stud to the adjacent one. You should be measuring between the inner edges of the studs. Write this number down, rounding to the nearest quarter inch. The firestopping blocks will be cut to fit this space.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pWvBEwRitbE</ref>
#*Before you begin, check to see if your the walls of your basement already have some form of firestopping in place.<ref>http://www.askthebuilder.com/fire-stop-construction/</ref>
#*Measure each stud spacing separately in case one or more of them happen to be slightly off.

#Cut 2x4s to fit the space between each stud. Acquire a set of 2” nominal lumber boards. Using the measurements of the stud spacing that you just took, saw the boards straight across width-wise. Take care to make the edges clean and even. The best way to do this is to use a circular saw that allows you to make precise cuts.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/tools/circular-saws/circular-saw-tips-and-techniques/view-all</ref>
#*To install firestops between every stud, you may need to use several boards.
#*You can also use 2x8s if a wider space exists between the studs and the foundation wall.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pWvBEwRitbE</ref>
#*Nominal lumber is one of a few firestopping materials approved by the IRC.

#Secure the firestopping blocks. Position the newly made blocks in the space at the top of the studs where they meet the floor joists or recessed wall frame, then nail them into place. Test the blocks to confirm that they’re firmly fastened.

#*The firestopping blocks act as a barrier to keep flames and combustible gases from rising to the upper levels of your home. Without them, hollow wall cavities are like chimneys, creating drafts that draw the fire upward.<ref>http://www.askthebuilder.com/fire-stop-construction/</ref>
#*Some homes utilize a double layer of firestopping for added protection. You might consider this approach should your space and materials allow it.

#Fill in the gaps with fireproof caulking. If there are any spaces remaining between the studs and the firestopping blocks, this will seal them and prevent drafts from forming and accelerating the spread of fire. Simply spray a thin line into whatever cracks and crevices you come across. As it dries, the caulk will expand inside the gaps, blocking them off and neutralizing airflow. <ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F9_fHgUx3b0</ref>
#*To be on the safe side, seal every space surrounding the blocks, including where the studs intersect the joists of the upper floor, no matter how small.

#Wall over the studs. Once the firestopping blocks have been successfully installed, you can proceed to cover the studs with plywood or drywall. This will create multiple separate compartments inside the wall rather than one large cavity. In the event of an emergency, each individual compartment will help stop or slow the spread of fire.<ref>http://www.askthebuilder.com/fire-stop-construction/</ref>
#*Oxygen will be unable to infiltrate the sealed compartments, effectively stifling the fire.
#*Patch holes opened by contractors and plumbers with fireproof building materials and sealants.
=== Making Use of Other Fireproofing Features ===

#Insulate your basement with fire-blocking materials. Insulators like gypsum, mineral wool and particle board are known for their fire-retardant qualities. If you’re in the process of building a new house, you probably won’t have to specify that you want fireproof materials, as these features are now standard. That being said, it never hurts to ask what types of materials are being used in the construction of your home.<ref>http://www.pdskc.org/portals/pdskc/documents/applications_forms/checklists/BasementHandout.pdf</ref>
#*Replace old and unsafe insulation with fire-rated materials as soon as it’s discovered.<ref>https://energy.gov/energysaver/insulation-materials</ref>
#*Installing fireproof insulation in older homes demands a lot of labor and expense, but it’s worth considering if you’re serious about safeguarding your family and property.

#Use fireproof caulking and adhesives. As mentioned, there are certain types of caulks, epoxies and other sealants used to stop up gaps in a home’s structure that have been approved for firestopping. It only takes a small amount to make problem areas fire-tight. Finishing your basement with a fireproof sealant is always a good idea, especially if your home has balloon framing or a similarly hollow construction that can create openings for drafts.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pWvBEwRitbE</ref>
#*Fireproof sealants are readily available at major home improvement stores.

#Invest in fire-safe windows. For basements with windows, you’ll want to shop around for styles that meet prescribed safety regulations, or that are made using fire-rated glass. These types of window glasses are treated with special compounds that reflect and disperse heat, making them less likely to shatter. With the right windows, you’ll be protected from fire whether it originates inside or outside.<ref>https://www.thisoldhouse.com/ideas/fire-resistant-doors-and-windows</ref>
#*One popular alternative to conventional windows is glass blocks or panels, which will allow natural light to filter into the basement without becoming a safety hazard.

#*It’s also critical that your basement present some clear and unobstructed means of escape in case a fire does break out. Your windows will need to be a particular size and easy to open without any screens, grills or other covers.<ref>http://news.nationalpost.com/homes/mike-holmes-how-to-turn-your-basement-into-a-proper-rental-apartment</ref>

#Install a home sprinkler system. While not a form of fireproofing in the traditional sense, a sprinkler system can stop flames in their tracks before they grow big enough to wreak havoc. Sprinklers trigger automatically when exposed to heat, meaning you don’t even have to be aware of a fire for them to do their job. This makes them an exceptional first line of defense against fires that start in the sublevels of your home.<ref>https://www.thisoldhouse.com/ideas/fire-resistant-insulation-and-systems</ref>
#*Get an estimate to see if it’s feasible to have water routed through a sprinkler system in your home.
#*If you do decide to put in a sprinkler system, don’t forget to clear your basement of any belongings that are vulnerable to water damage.

#Have your wiring inspected regularly. Faulty electrical wiring is one of the leading causes of household fires. Schedule an inspection at least once a year to to ensure that your home’s wiring is safe. In the meantime, be on the lookout for fraying, splitting, shorting and other electrical risks that could potentially lead to a fire.<ref>https://sewelldirect.com/learning-center/cable-fire-safety</ref>
#*Remember: when it comes to accidents and disasters, prevention is the best solution.

#*If your home is more than a few decades old, or you experience electrical problems with abnormal frequency, it may be time to have it rewired.<ref>https://sewelldirect.com/learning-center/cable-fire-safety</ref>
== Tips ==
*Most updated building codes require that the basement of a new home be properly fireproofed. Check to see if this is the case with your home before embarking on an involved DIY project.

*In some instances, you may be able to find specially designed firestopping blocks made from fire-resistant foam. These can save you the trouble of having to do a lot of measuring and sawing, but they’ll likely cost more than using wood.
*Purchase fire guards to go on the outside of your home’s light switches and electrical outlets.
*If you have any questions about the methods or materials used to fireproof your basement, don’t hesitate to speak to a contractor, building inspector or firefighter.
== Warnings ==

*If you plan on installing firestopping blocks yourself, make sure they meet building code standards. Otherwise, you could be in violation of the law and, even worse, be left without functioning fireproofing.
== Things You'll Need ==
*2x4 or 2x8 nominal lumber boards
*Circular saw
*Tape measure
*Hammer and nails
*Fire-rated particle board or plywood
*Fireproof caulking and other sealants and adhesives
*Fireproof insulating materials
*Home sprinkler system
